cards.rationale: Exact preimage/candidate canonical hashes and live baseline verified. Polybius Histories 18.29–30 says pikes in ranks 2–5 extended beyond the front rank, while the more distant ranks held theirs slanting over the troops ahead; the candidate correctly identifies the Macedonian phalanx. The four options are distinct formations or force types, and the notes support their own choices. The number of pike ranks makes medium difficulty reasonable. The sibling military cards describe separate formation or equipment facts, not this five-rank feature.

Exact hashes verified. Pliny Natural History 10.4 (the source paragraph following the eagle section) says Marius in his second consulship prescribed the eagle alone as the Roman legions’ standard and rejected the four other animal emblems. This supports the key and explanation; wording about the eagle becoming the sole animal image is a faithful short paraphrase. All four choices are Roman military subdivisions/units. Polybius 6.24–27 supports the notes about maniples, legions and turmae; Caesar Gallic War 7.65 supports the cohort note. Medium suits a specific historical source fact. No catalog card repeats Marius’s standard reform.

Exact hashes verified. Attic Inscriptions Online SEG 21.525 lines 3–10 names the hipparchs and tribal cavalry commanders, their register, appointment of another hundred cavalry and a current total of three hundred. This supports prompt and explanation. The distractors are plausible ancient force categories; notes match Xenophon’s Rhodian slingers, Arrian’s horse-to-foot remounting, Caesar’s British chariots and Polybius’s elephant river crossing. The historical decree clue merits medium difficulty. General catalog mentions of horse scrutiny or cavalry do not give this inscription’s increase and total.

Exact hashes verified. Arrian Anabasis V.15 reports Porus put elephants about one hundred feet apart before the infantry to protect it and frighten Alexander’s cavalry; the candidate accurately compresses that arrangement. The explanation’s claim about intimidating horses is explicit in the source. Options are plausible ancient force types; their notes cite separate facts. Medium is right for a specific battle deployment. No other catalog card supplies this Porus/Hydaspes formation detail.

Exact hashes verified. NYU ISAW’s object record calls the object a double spherical sundial, gives white marble, gymnasium at Delos and ca. 2nd century BCE; its caption/photo description shows two opposite carved hemispheres. Prompt and explanation fit that artifact. The four answers are recognizable time/astronomical instruments; the object clues are specific but solvable at easy level. Notes are supported by UCL, Oxford HSM and the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project. The Delos mythology card associates the island with Apollo and Artemis but no instrument; the Antikythera card tests a Metonic calendar ratio. Current rows 044–045 (lunar month/intercalation) are calendar concepts, not clues to the Delos dial. The broad sundial prompt in this target’s preimage is not a separate sibling and is replaced by this artifact-level candidate.

Exact hashes verified. Vitruvius On Architecture 9.8.2–6 (Morris Hicky Morgan translation of the primary text) attributes water-clock methods to Ctesibius, says regular water flow raises the float, gearing transmits the motion and a figure emerges to point to hours on a column. Prompt and explanation accurately summarize it; “the figure rose” is consistent with the described emergence/movement. Answer choices are parallel time/astronomy instruments; the source-specific mechanism makes medium appropriate. UCL supports the Karnak water-clock note, Oxford supports the sundial/astrolabe notes, and the research project supports Antikythera eclipse prediction. Current rows 044–045 test lunar month/intercalation, not the Ctesibius mechanism. The broad water-clock prompt in this target’s preimage is replaced rather than a separate sibling dependency.
